attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, written in his voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the factual core: products are unprofitable, unreliable and prone to hallucination, and Sora is too costly for poor results. Leaving out 'deeply boring' and the hype framing is acceptable.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'unprofitable products' as product-level economics, using calendar 2024, is ordinary and not stretched. Opinion words are not given numeric thresholds. The result depends on accounting and cost-allocation choices the speaker never supplied.

evidence.note: A 2024 SimpleQA paper evaluates models from both companies and documents hallucinations. It supports only the hallucination part and says nothing on profitability.

OpenAI's December 2024 Sora launch post admits physics and long-action limitations and says affordability is still being worked on. This partly supports the quality point but gives no training or serving costs.

Unverified estimates of OpenAI's API gross margin for mid-2024. They cover gross, not net, margins and only one product line, so they are context. They neither establish nor refute product-level net profitability.

reviews.rationale: The hallucination and unreliability part has support (e1, plus e2 for Sora quality). The core claims are product-level net unprofitability for both companies and Sora's cost relative to its output. No product-level accounts or Sora cost data are in the packet, and the API gross-margin estimate is unverified and on a different basis. The evidence does not settle the full claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition captures both parts: no massive new data centers are needed, and no endless supply of ever-bigger GPUs is needed to progress. The point about austere hardware is implied.

contract.note: Reading the claim as technical necessity for the V3/R1 generation in the release window is the ordinary present-tense meaning. It sensibly declines to treat 'to progress' as a guarantee of unlimited future progress.

evidence.note: DeepSeek's V3 report says training used 2048 H800s, which is existing, non-frontier hardware. This is a company disclosure, so it is not an independent check of training hardware.

On 27 January 2025, Unsloth independently showed the full R1 running quantized on ordinary GPUs or with CPU offload. It is slower and loses some quality, but it supports running on existing and more austere hardware.
Shows progress through distillation into smaller models. These are distinct from full R1, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: An independent demonstration (e9) shows the full R1 running on existing and modest hardware. DeepSeek's report (e8) describes training V3 on a 2048-GPU H800 cluster with software efficiency gains, which is neither a massive new facility nor a next-generation GPU. The packet contains no counterevidence of technical necessity. One caveat: the training-hardware figure comes from the company itself.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'right now', the belief framing, and the difference between 'no companies' and 'not many' use cases. Its wording ('he does not believe') reads like a statement about his mental state, but the contract correctly scores it as an assessment of the world.

contract.note: Treating 'I do not believe' as a firm assessment is fair: it is not graded probability language. Separating model-provider prices from wider adoption costs follows his wording about OpenAI's pricing. The January 2025 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: An October 2024 IDC survey of 70 executives on general genAI adoption costs. It does not isolate model-provider prices or document blocked deployments in January 2025.
A January 2024 report that enterprises avoided GPT-4 as too expensive or slow. It is a year before the claim, cites speed as well as price, and describes switching models, not blocked deployment.

reviews.rationale: Neither item documents a company deployment blocked by model-provider pricing in January 2025, and neither measures how common that was. e1 combines broad adoption costs. e2 predates the period and describes model selection. The evidence neither confirms nor refutes the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition captures both firm assertions. It drops the 'I don't think' framing, but that is a firm stance, not graded probability. The parenthetical about o1 use cases is reasonably left out.

contract.note: Reading 'anyone' at face value, so that it includes professional non-adopters, and counting cost as a contributing reason follows his own universal wording. The surrounding text is about companies, so a narrower reading is possible. The result depends on this choice.

evidence.note: A 2024 survey of arbitrators found 7% of non-users cited cost as a factor in not using genAI. That contradicts 'anyone' under the contract. It was published by March 2025, before the evaluation date, and concerns the earlier period.
The R1 abstract says it performs comparably to o1 on reasoning tasks. That fits 'no new functionality' but does not establish it.

reviews.rationale: The first clause is a universal: no one has stayed out because of costs. A survey of non-users documents people citing cost as a reason for non-adoption, which contradicts it under the contract's reading. The functionality clause is unresolved because no full feature comparison exists. The joint proposition is therefore contradicted through its first clause.
